nodes.label: perovskite_definition
nodes.title: Perovskite material definition
nodes.content: Solution-processable organic-inorganic hybrid perovskites have the general formula CH3NH3PbX3 where X = Cl, Br, or I, and have attracted attention as light-harvesting materials for mesoscopic solar cells [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: prior_work_limitation
nodes.title: Single-step deposition produces morphological variability
nodes.content: The single-step deposition of perovskite pigment onto mesoporous metal oxide films using a mixture of PbX2 and CH3NH3X in a common solvent produces large morphological variations, resulting in a wide spread of photovoltaic performance in the resulting devices [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: sequential_deposition_introduced
nodes.title: Sequential deposition method introduced
nodes.content: A sequential deposition method is introduced for the formation of the perovskite pigment within the porous metal oxide film: PbI2 is first introduced from solution into a nanoporous titanium dioxide film and subsequently transformed into the perovskite by exposing it to a solution of CH3NH3I [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Core method clearly described in paper.

nodes.label: control_improvement
nodes.title: Sequential method improves morphology control
nodes.content: The sequential deposition method permits much better control over perovskite morphology than the previously employed single-step route [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: efficiency_achieved
nodes.title: 15% efficiency achieved with sequential deposition
nodes.content: Using the sequential deposition technique for solid-state mesoscopic solar cells, a power conversion efficiency of approximately 15% is achieved under standard AM1.5G test conditions [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: reproducibility_improvement
nodes.title: Sequential method improves reproducibility
nodes.content: The sequential deposition method greatly increases the reproducibility of photovoltaic performance compared to single-step deposition [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: device_structure
nodes.title: Device structure configuration
nodes.content: The photovoltaic device structure consists of: FTO-coated glass substrate (front contact), 30-40 nm TiO2 compact layer (aerosol spray pyrolysis), 350 nm mesoporous TiO2 layer (20-nm-sized anatase particles), perovskite infiltrant, spiro-MeOTAD hole-transporting material (HTM), and 80 nm Au back contact [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: mesoporous_tio2_deposition
nodes.title: Mesoporous TiO2 deposition protocol
nodes.content: Mesoporous TiO2 films composed of 20-nm-sized particles are deposited by spin coating at 5,000 rpm for 30 s using TiO2 paste (Dyesol 18NRT) diluted in ethanol (2:7 weight ratio), followed by drying at 125 C and annealing at 500 C for 15 min [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: pbi2_infiltration
nodes.title: PbI2 infiltration protocol
nodes.content: PbI2 is dissolved in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) at a concentration of 462 mg/ml (~1 M) under stirring at 70 C. The mesoporous TiO2 films are infiltrated by spin coating at 6,500 rpm for 90 s, then dried at 70 C for 30 min [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: mai_conversion
nodes.title: Methylammonium iodide conversion protocol
nodes.content: After PbI2 infiltration, films are dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol (10 mg/ml) for 20 s, rinsed with 2-propanol, and dried at 70 C for 30 min to convert PbI2 to CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: htm_deposition
nodes.title: HTM spin-coating formulation
nodes.content: The HTM is deposited by spin coating at 4,000 rpm for 30 s using a solution of spiro-MeOTAD (72.3 mg), 4-tert-butylpyridine (28.8 ul), lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulphonyl)imide (17.5 ul of 520 mg/ml in acetonitrile), and Co(III) dopant (29 ul of 300 mg/ml in acetonitrile) in 1 ml chlorobenzene [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: best_device_modification
nodes.title: Modified conditions for best-performing devices
nodes.content: For the best-performing devices (15% PCE), the PbI2 is spin-cast at 6,500 rpm for 5 s (instead of 90 s), and samples are pre-wetted by dipping in 2-propanol for 1-2 s before the CH3NH3I conversion step [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct description of modified conditions: shorter spin-cast and pre-wetting.

nodes.label: j_v_measurement
nodes.title: J-V characterization method
nodes.content: Current-voltage characteristics are measured under simulated AM1.5G solar irradiation using a 450 W xenon lamp with Schott K113 Tempax sunlight filter. Light intensity is calibrated using a calibrated Si reference diode with KG-3 infrared cut-off filter. Devices are measured using a 0.285 cm^2 metal aperture [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: ipce_measurement
nodes.title: IPCE measurement method
nodes.content: IPCE spectra are recorded as functions of wavelength under constant white light bias (approximately 5 mW/cm^2) from an array of white LEDs. The excitation beam from a 300 W xenon lamp is focused through a Gemini-180 double monochromator and chopped at approximately 2 Hz, detected with an SR830 DSP Lock-In Amplifier [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: stability_testing
nodes.title: Long-term stability test protocol
nodes.content: For long-term stability tests, devices are sealed in argon using a 50-mm-thick hot-melting polymer and microscope coverslip. Devices are subjected to constant light soaking at approximately 100 mW/cm^2 using white LED array (Philips LXM3-PW51 4000K), maintained at maximum power point, at approximately 45 C. J-V measurements at different light intensities are recorded automatically every 2 h [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: optical_spectroscopy
nodes.title: Optical spectroscopy methods
nodes.content: Optical absorption measurements are carried out using a Varian Cary 5 spectrophotometer. Photoluminescence is measured on a Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorolog spectrofluorometer. Samples are placed vertically in a 10 mm path length cuvette [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: xrd_measurement
nodes.title: XRD measurement parameters
nodes.content: X-ray powder diagrams are recorded on an X'Pert MPD PRO (PANalytical) with Cu anode (lambda = 1.54060 A), graphite (002) monochromator, and RTMS X'Celerator detector in BRAGG-BRENTANO geometry. Step size is 0.008 deg with acquisition time up to 7.5 min/deg [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: pbi2_complete_infiltration
nodes.title: PbI2 completely contained within TiO2 nanopores
nodes.content: PbI2 infiltration into mesoporous TiO2 films is complete: cross-sectional SEM shows no PbI2 crystals protruding from the surface of the mesoporous anatase layer, indicating the PbI2 is entirely contained within the nanopores of the TiO2 film [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 1a | Cross-sectional SEM of mesoporous TiO2 film infiltrated with PbI2
metadata.prior_justification: Direct SEM observation showing complete PbI2 infiltration into TiO2 nanopores.

nodes.label: pbi2_crystal_size
nodes.title: PbI2 crystal size limited to ~22 nm in nanopores
nodes.content: When confined within mesoporous TiO2 scaffold, PbI2 crystal size is limited to approximately 22 nm by the pore size of the host [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Crystal size (~22 nm) measured from pore size constraint.

nodes.label: color_change_observed
nodes.title: Color change indicates rapid perovskite formation
nodes.content: Dipping the TiO2/PbI2 composite film into CH3NH3I solution (10 mg/ml in 2-propanol) immediately changes its color from yellow to dark brown, indicating formation of CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: absorption_increase
nodes.title: Perovskite absorption increase complete within seconds
nodes.content: The increase in perovskite absorption at 550 nm during conversion is practically complete within a few seconds of exposing the PbI2-loaded TiO2 film to the CH3NH3I solution. A small additional increase occurring on a timescale of 100 s contributes only a few percent to the total signal and is attributed to morphological changes producing enhanced light scattering [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 1b | Change in absorbance at 550 nm during transformation

nodes.label: pl_quenching_pbi2
nodes.title: PbI2 photoluminescence quenched during conversion
nodes.content: The conversion is accompanied by quenching of PbI2 emission at 425 nm, confirming PbI2 consumption during the reaction with CH3NH3I [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 1c | Change in PL intensity at 520 nm during transformation (PbI2 quenching)

nodes.label: perovskite_pl_increase
nodes.title: Perovskite emission at 775 nm increases then decreases
nodes.content: The perovskite luminescence at 775 nm increases concomitantly with conversion, passing through a maximum before decreasing to a stationary value due to self-absorption by the perovskite formed during the reaction [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 1d | Change in PL intensity at 775 nm during transformation

nodes.label: pbi2_tio2_orientation
nodes.title: Mesoporous TiO2 induces different PbI2 crystal orientation
nodes.content: PbI2 loaded on mesoporous TiO2 shows three additional diffraction peaks (not present for flat glass) that suggest the anatase scaffold induces a different orientation for PbI2 crystal growth, with peaks attributed to the (110) and (111) lattice planes of the 2H polytype and a third peak assigned to a different PbI2 variant [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 1e | XRD spectra showing PbI2 orientation differences

nodes.label: perovskite_xrd_confirmed
nodes.title: Tetragonal perovskite XRD peaks observed after conversion
nodes.content: XRD shows new diffraction peaks after CH3NH3I reaction that are in good agreement with literature data on the tetragonal phase of CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite, confirming complete conversion within the mesoporous TiO2 scaffold [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct XRD measurement showing tetragonal perovskite peaks after conversion.

nodes.label: flat_substrate_incomplete_conversion
nodes.title: Flat substrate shows incomplete perovskite conversion
nodes.content: On flat glass substrate, conversion of PbI2 to perovskite is incomplete; a large amount of unreacted PbI2 remains even after a dipping time of 45 min, with CH3NH3I insertion hardly proceeding beyond the surface of thin PbI2 films [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct XRD observation of unreacted PbI2 after 45 min on flat glass.

nodes.label: conversion_rate_enhancement
nodes.title: Nanoscopic confinement dramatically accelerates conversion
nodes.content: Confining PbI2 crystals to approximately 22 nm within mesoporous TiO2 drastically enhances their rate of conversion to perovskite, completing within a few seconds of contact with methylammonium iodide solution. In contrast, flat surface deposition produces larger 50-200 nm crystallites resulting in incomplete conversion [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: nanomorphology_enforced
nodes.title: Mesoporous scaffold enforces perovskite nanomorphology
nodes.content: The mesoporous TiO2 scaffold forces the perovskite to adopt a confined nanomorphology dictated by the pore structure [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: typical_device_performance
nodes.title: Typical device performance: 12.9% PCE
nodes.content: A typical photovoltaic device measured at 95.6 mW/cm^2 shows: short-circuit photocurrent Jsc = 17.1 mA/cm^2, open-circuit voltage Voc = 992 mV, fill factor = 0.73, yielding a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 12.9% [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 3a | J-V curves for typical photovoltaic device

nodes.label: device_batch_statistics
nodes.title: Batch average PCE: 12.0% +/- 0.5%
nodes.content: Statistical data from a batch of ten photovoltaic devices shows an average PCE of 12.0% with a standard deviation of 0.5%, demonstrating high reproducibility [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct experimental measurement from 10 devices: average PCE 12.0% +/- 0.5%.

nodes.label: ipce_onset
nodes.title: IPCE onset at 800 nm matches perovskite bandgap
nodes.content: IPCE shows photocurrent generation starting at 800 nm, consistent with the bandgap of CH3NH3PbI3 [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: ipce_peak_value
nodes.title: IPCE peak exceeds 90% in short wavelengths
nodes.content: IPCE reaches peak values of over 90% in the short-wavelength region of the visible spectrum [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 3b | IPCE spectrum
metadata.prior_justification: Direct IPCE measurement showing peak values exceeding 90%.

nodes.label: integrated_current_match
nodes.title: Integrated IPCE current matches measured Jsc
nodes.content: Integrating the overlap of the IPCE spectrum with the AM1.5G solar photon flux yields a current density of 18.4 mA/cm^2, in excellent agreement with the measured photocurrent density extrapolated to 17.9 mA/cm^2 at standard AM1.5G intensity of 100 mW/cm^2. This confirms negligible mismatch between simulated sunlight and AM1.5G standard [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: lhe_data
nodes.title: Low IPCE in 600-800 nm due to reduced light harvesting
nodes.content: The low IPCE values in the 600-800 nm range result from the smaller absorption of the perovskite in this spectral region, as shown by the light-harvesting efficiency (LHE) spectrum [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: apce_exceeds_90_percent
nodes.title: APCE exceeds 90% indicating near-unity quantum yield
nodes.content: The absorbed-photon-to-current conversion efficiency (APCE) derived from IPCE and LHE is greater than 90% over the whole visible region (without correction for reflective losses), indicating near-unity quantum yield for charge carrier generation and collection [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 3d | APCE spectrum
metadata.prior_justification: Direct measurement showing APCE >90% across visible range without correction for reflective losses.

nodes.label: best_device_performance
nodes.title: Best device: 15.0% PCE
nodes.content: The best-performing cell (fabricated with modified conditions) shows: Jsc = 20.0 mA/cm^2, Voc = 993 mV, fill factor = 0.73, yielding a PCE of 15.0% measured at 96.4 mW/cm^2. Several cells achieved PCEs between 14% and 15% [@Burschka2013].

metadata.caption: Figure 3e | J-V curves for best-performing cell

nodes.label: certified_efficiency
nodes.title: Certified PCE: 14.14%
nodes.content: One of the best-performing devices was sent to an accredited photovoltaic calibration laboratory for certification, confirming a power conversion efficiency of 14.14% under standard AM1.5G reporting conditions [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: best_device_improvement_attributed
nodes.title: Higher photocurrent from increased loading and light scattering
nodes.content: The significantly higher photocurrent in top-performance devices is attributed to increased loading of the porous TiO2 film with perovskite pigment and increased light scattering from the pre-wetting step, improving the long-wavelength response of the cell [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Attribution supported by pre-wetting modification and spectral response changes.

nodes.label: stability_result
nodes.title: Device retains >80% PCE after 500 hours
nodes.content: A sealed photovoltaic device maintained more than 80% of its initial PCE after 500 hours of continuous light soaking at approximately 100 mW/cm^2 and 45 C under argon atmosphere with maximum power point tracking [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct 500-hour stability test: device retains >80% of initial PCE.

nodes.label: no_photodegradation
nodes.title: No photodegradation observed
nodes.content: No change in short-circuit photocurrent is observed during the 500-hour stability test, indicating no photodegradation of the perovskite light harvester [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Direct observation of unchanged Jsc during stability test.

nodes.label: pce_decrease_mechanism
nodes.title: PCE decrease due to Voc and FF reduction from shunt resistance loss
nodes.content: The decrease in PCE during stability testing is due only to decreases in open-circuit voltage and fill factor, with similar decay shapes suggesting a linked degradation mechanism attributed mainly to a decrease in shunt resistance [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: conversion_facilitation
nodes.title: Nanoporous confinement facilitates perovskite conversion
nodes.content: The confinement of PbI2 within the nanoporous TiO2 network greatly facilitates its conversion to the perovskite pigment, compared to flat substrate deposition [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: nanomorphology_enforcement
nodes.title: Mesoporous scaffold enforces perovskite nanomorphology
nodes.content: The mesoporous scaffold forces the perovskite to adopt a confined nanomorphology [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: layered_pbi2_structure
nodes.title: Layered PbI2 structure enables cation insertion
nodes.content: The insertion of the organic cation is facilitated through the layered PbI2 structure, which consists of three spatially repeating planes: I-Pb-I. Strong intralayer chemical bonding combined with weak interlayer van der Waals interactions allows easy insertion of guest molecules between the layers [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Well-established in literature on polytypism and intercalation.

nodes.label: thermodynamic_driving_force
nodes.title: Lattice energy difference drives conversion
nodes.content: The thermodynamic driving force for the two-step conversion is the difference in bulk lattice energy between PbI2 and CH3NH3PbI3, with the initial crystal lattice serving as a template for the formation of the desired compound. This is analogous to ion exchange reactions used to convert II-V semiconductor nanocrystals to III-V analogues while preserving particle size and distribution [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Established principle from semiconductor nanocrystal ion exchange literature.

nodes.label: reaction_kinetics_enhancement
nodes.title: Nanoscopic morphology combined with high formation energy enhances kinetics
nodes.content: The large energy of formation of the hybrid perovskite combined with the nanoscopic morphology of the PbI2 precursor (approximately 22 nm crystals) greatly enhances reaction kinetics, enabling complete transformation within seconds of contact with methylammonium iodide solution [@Burschka2013].

metadata.prior_justification: Reasonable mechanistic interpretation combining formation energy and nanoscale morphology.

nodes.label: two_step_method_applicability
nodes.title: Sequential deposition applicable to other metal halide mesostructures
nodes.content: The two-step sequential deposition method is applicable to other preformed metal halide mesostructures that can be converted into the desired perovskite by insertion reactions [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: record_efficiency
nodes.title: 15% PCE sets record for solution-processed photovoltaics
nodes.content: The power conversion efficiency of 15% achieved with the best device is amongst the highest for solution-processed photovoltaics and sets a new record for organic or hybrid inorganic-organic solar cells at the time of publication [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: reproducibility_demonstrated
nodes.title: Method enables reproducible high performance
nodes.content: The sequential deposition method provides a means to achieve excellent photovoltaic performance with high reproducibility, addressing the wide spread of performance characteristic of single-step deposition methods [@Burschka2013].

nodes.label: future_potential
nodes.title: Perovskite photovoltaics may rival silicon
nodes.content: Perovskite-based photovoltaic devices fabricated using this method have potential for widespread application and may eventually rival conventional silicon-based photovoltaics [@Burschka2013].
